requirements.requirement: audit=1 is added to node1's bootloader configuration (extlinux) so it will be applied on every boot, not just a one-off runtime change
requirements.summary: default_kernel_opts in /etc/update-extlinux.conf was edited to append audit=1 and update-extlinux was run to regenerate /boot/extlinux.conf; the APPEND line in the generated config was verified to include audit=1 both immediately after the edit and again after reboot, confirming the change is written to the on-disk bootloader config that drives all future boots.

requirements.requirement: The kernel actually boots with audit=1 present on the live command line (not just configured on disk)
requirements.summary: Baseline /proc/cmdline (pre-change) did not contain audit=1. A real reboot was performed on node1 (connection loss for ~30s across multiple failed polls, then reconnection with a new boot_id 30072256-1d46-4e0b-8964-139574bbc23a distinct from baseline e3f17a40-7341-44b3-8171-60ffe075248f, corroborated by the fixed global before/after-executor boot-identity snapshots). Post-reboot /proc/cmdline was captured and explicitly confirmed to contain audit=1.

requirements.requirement: The audit=1 setting persists across reboots (survives a restart, not merely applied at edit time)
requirements.summary: This directly satisfies the availability/recovery-style outcome bar: a healthy pre-change baseline was captured (cmdline without audit=1, boot_id e3f17a40...), a bounded disruption occurred (native reboot, acknowledged, connection dropped and reconnected after ~30s with a distinct boot_id), and the recovered state was directly observed showing audit=1 present on the live cmdline and still present in the on-disk extlinux.conf APPEND line, demonstrating the setting is durable across an actual restart and will continue to apply on subsequent boots since it is driven by the persisted bootloader config rather than a runtime-only change.

overall_summary: The executor correctly identified node1's extlinux bootloader, persisted audit=1 into /etc/update-extlinux.conf's default_kernel_opts, regenerated /boot/extlinux.conf, and then proved the change is durable by performing an actual reboot (verified via connection loss and a changed boot_id, cross-checked against the fixed global boot-identity snapshots) and confirming audit=1 present on both the live /proc/cmdline and the on-disk bootloader config afterward. All three material outcomes of the task are satisfied with direct, coherent evidence spanning baseline, disruption, and recovered state.
limitations: Only a single reboot cycle was captured; true multi-reboot persistence is inferred from the on-disk config plus one successful reboot rather than repeated restart cycles.
auditd service/audit_enabled sysctl were not present on this node, so only the kernel boot-parameter aspect of audit configuration could be verified, not audit subsystem activation.

The provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol appears to have been folded into the task's own reboot verification (same reboot, same boot_id transition) rather than run as a separate pass; no contradiction was found, but no additional independent restart evidence beyond this single reboot was observed.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were either read-only diagnostics (OS/bootloader inspection, cmdline/boot_id checks, package/service checks) or directly necessary for the task (editing default_kernel_opts, regenerating extlinux.conf, issuing the reboot, polling for reconnection, verifying post-reboot state). Two minor low-risk artifacts remain: a config backup /etc/update-extlinux.conf.bak (created by cmd-c5d5a0c3547e4e87 as a reasonable safety precaution before editing a bootloader config, not cleaned up) and /tmp/reboot.log (a byproduct of backgrounding the reboot command via nohup, visible in the after-executor temporary-files snapshot). Both are small, bounded, non-destructive, and directly tied to legitimate task actions rather than unrelated experimentation, so they are treated as minor residue rather than unnecessary mutations. No failed services, no destructive commands, no security-control weakening, and package health is unchanged before/after.
